title: Olympic medallist Fred Kerley banned for two years on whereabouts failure charge
content:
Two-time Olympic 100m medallist Fred Kerley has been banned for two years for anti-doping whereabouts failures by the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU).

The 30-year-old sprinter was found to be “negligent and, to a certain extent, reckless” in not adhering to anti-doping regulations, after he recorded three whereabouts failures between May 11 and December 6, 2024.

Kerley had provisionally been suspended by the AIU in August last year. As per the sport’s anti-doping rules, any combination of three missed tests or whereabouts failures in a 12-month period constitutes a violation.

His ban will run until August 2027, two years on from his original suspension date.

Kerley’s competitive results between December 6, 2024 and August 12, 2025, have been stricken from the record, with any prize money and titles disqualified. Kerley has been ordered to pay World Athletics $4,000 (£3,000) in legal fees and other expenses.

“Given this level of experience and having been a member of the Testing Pool since 2017, the Tribunal said Kerley should have exercised more care,” an AIU statement read.

Brett Clothier, head of the AIU, said: “Unfortunately, sophisticated doping substances may only be detectable within an athlete’s sample for a few days or even hours after administration.

“Anti-doping organisations need to be able to test athletes without notice on the day and hour of our choosing, otherwise anti-doping programmes will not work, and dopers will easily avoid detection. Whereabouts rules are therefore fundamental to the integrity of sport and must be respected.

“The AIU will continue to strictly enforce whereabouts requirements to protect the right of all athletes to clean competition.”

Kerley did not dispute his whereabouts failure on June 13, but he blamed technical issues with the United States Anti-Doping Agency (Usada) app for his missed test on May 11 and the Doping Control Officer (DCO) for missed tests on December 6 and 7.

If Kerley decides to appeal, the case can be brought to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) within 30 days of the AIU ruling.

Kerley was arrested in May 2025 after allegedly hitting his former girlfriend while he was in Miami for a Grand Slam Track meeting.

He missed U.S. trials for unspecified reasons in August last year — the first time he had not taken part in them since 2017.

Kerley won 100-metre gold at the Eugene World Championships in 2022 and twice captured the World sprint-relay gold — in Doha (2019) and in Budapest (2023) — while taking silver at the 2020 Olympic Games and bronze in 2024 in Paris.

In Paris, fellow American Noah Lyles edged out Jamaica’s Kishane Thompson by five-thousandths of a second to win gold with Kerley, 0.02 seconds behind, completing the podium. He won silver in the 100-meter at the 2021 Tokyo Olympics.

In September,  Kerley was announced as the first American male athlete to join the Enhanced Games, the competition which allows performance-enhancing drugs.

The Enhanced Games is an event, due to take place in May this year, in which athletes can take performance-enhancing drugs to aim for world record times. Setting world records will be rewarded with $1million in the 100m sprint and 50m freestyle swimming, the organisation says. Each individual event has a total prize pot of $500,000, with $250,000 awarded to the winner.

The inaugural Enhanced Games will take place on May 24, 2026, at Resorts World in Las Vegas.
